    Evaluate ∣6−473∣\begin{vmatrix} 6 & -4 \\ 7 & 3 \end{vmatrix}​67​−43​​.

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Adds the anti-diagonal product instead of subtracting it, giving 18+(−28)18 + (-28)18+(−28).

    You chose B: Multiplies down each column, 6×76 \times 76×7 against −4×3-4 \times 3−4×3, rather than along the diagonals.

    You chose D: Takes anti-diagonal minus main diagonal, which reverses the sign of the whole answer.

    Multiply down the main diagonal, then subtract the product up the anti-diagonal. The entry −4-4−4 carries its sign into that second product, so subtracting −28-28−28 adds.

    ∣6−473∣=(6)(3)−(−4)(7)=18+28=46\begin{vmatrix} 6 & -4 \\ 7 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = (6)(3) - (-4)(7) = 18 + 28 = 46​67​−43​​=(6)(3)−(−4)(7)=18+28=46

    Which description fits the graph of the solution set of 4x−3y≤−124x - 3y \le -124x−3y≤−12?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Substitutes the origin but shades the side it sits on even though 0≤−120 \le -120≤−12 came out false.

    You chose C: Draws the boundary dashed, as though ≤\le≤ excluded the line, when equality is one of the cases it allows.

    You chose D: Reads the side straight off the symbol as below and to the left, where the origin sits, and excludes the boundary as well.

    The symbol ≤\le≤ allows equality, so the points of the line 4x−3y=−124x - 3y = -124x−3y=−12 are solutions and the boundary is drawn solid. One point off the line then settles the side, and the origin fails, so the shading goes on the other side.

    4(0)−3(0)=0,0≤−12 is false4(0) - 3(0) = 0, \qquad 0 \le -12 \text{ is false}4(0)−3(0)=0,0≤−12 is false

    How many pairs (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) satisfy both 10x−4y=1410x - 4y = 1410x−4y=14 and −15x+6y=−20-15x + 6y = -20−15x+6y=−20?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Compares the leading coefficients 101010 and −15-15−15 alone and reads unlike numbers as unlike ratios.

    You chose B: Sees the coefficient ratios agree and calls the second equation a rescaling of the first, without checking whether the constants keep the pattern.

    You chose C: Collects one solution from each equation, as though a system's solutions were gathered rather than shared.

    Both equations are already in standard form, so compare the three ratios in turn. The coefficient ratios agree, which rules out a single crossing point, and then the constants decide between parallel and coincident.

    10−15=−23=−46,14−20=−710\frac{10}{-15} = -\frac{2}{3} = \frac{-4}{6}, \qquad \frac{14}{-20} = -\frac{7}{10}−1510​=−32​=6−4​,−2014​=−107​

    The constant ratio breaks the pattern, so the lines are parallel and share no point.

    A system has been reduced to the triangular form x+3y−z=7x + 3y - z = 7x+3y−z=7, 2y+5z=−62y + 5z = -62y+5z=−6, −4z=8-4z = 8−4z=8. What is xxx?

    Answer choices for question 5

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Substitutes z=−2z = -2z=−2 into the top row as +z+z+z, so the row reads x+6−2=7x + 6 - 2 = 7x+6−2=7.

    You chose C: Carries zzz up into the top row but leaves the 3y3y3y term behind, solving x+2=7x + 2 = 7x+2=7.

    You chose D: Climbs only as far as the middle row and reports the value that row produced.

    Climb from the bottom row, one new unknown at a time. The top row subtracts zzz, and zzz is negative, so that term arrives as +2+2+2.

    −4z=8⇒z=−2,2y+5(−2)=−6⇒y=2,x+3(2)−(−2)=7⇒x=−1-4z = 8 \Rightarrow z = -2, \qquad 2y + 5(-2) = -6 \Rightarrow y = 2, \qquad x + 3(2) - (-2) = 7 \Rightarrow x = -1−4z=8⇒z=−2,2y+5(−2)=−6⇒y=2,x+3(2)−(−2)=7⇒x=−1

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Adds all three first-row terms, so the middle one is not subtracted: −20+57+8-20 + 57 + 8−20+57+8.

    You chose B: Evaluates each minor as anti-diagonal minus main diagonal, which flips the sign of every term and so of the whole answer.

    You chose C: Extends the two by two diagonal rule straight to three rows, taking 2×0×62 \times 0 \times 62×0×6 minus 1×0×11 \times 0 \times 11×0×1.

    2(0−10)−3(24−5)+1(8−0)=−20−57+8=−692(0 - 10) - 3(24 - 5) + 1(8 - 0) = -20 - 57 + 8 = -692(0−10)−3(24−5)+1(8−0)=−20−57+8=−69

    A three-equation system in xxx, yyy and zzz is swept forward. One combination of its rows collapses to 0=00 = 00=0, and a different combination collapses to 0=90 = 90=9. What is its solution set?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Lets the vanishing row set the verdict, as though a redundant equation could free a variable while a false row still stands.

    You chose B: Counts only one surviving constraint because two rows collapsed, without noticing that one of them collapsed to a falsehood.

    You chose D: Treats 0=90 = 90=9 as an arithmetic slip to be hunted down rather than as the report it is, and expects the usual single triple.

    Read the two endings separately. A vanishing row is an equation that restated the others, so it constrains nothing at all; a false row is a demand no triple can meet.

    0=0 constrains nothing,0=9 is impossible0 = 0 \ \text{constrains nothing}, \qquad 0 = 9 \ \text{is impossible}0=0 constrains nothing,0=9 is impossible

    One row that cannot be satisfied empties the solution set however many other rows vanished, so nothing survives.

    A system in xxx, yyy and zzz reduces to x−2z=5x - 2z = 5x−2z=5 and y+4z=−3y + 4z = -3y+4z=−3, with its third row vanishing. Writing z=tz = tz=t, which family gives every solution?

    Answer choices for question 8

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Moves each term in zzz across the equals sign without changing its sign.

    You chose C: Solves both rows with the constants dropped, keeping only the terms that carry the parameter.

    You chose D: Reports the single triple at t=0t = 0t=0 instead of the whole family it belongs to.

    One row vanished, so two constraints remain in three unknowns and one variable is free. Solve each surviving row for its own leading variable with z=tz = tz=t in place.

    x=5+2t,y=−3−4t,z=tx = 5 + 2t, \qquad y = -3 - 4t, \qquad z = tx=5+2t,y=−3−4t,z=t

    Substituting back returns x−2t=5x - 2t = 5x−2t=5 and y+4t=−3y + 4t = -3y+4t=−3 for every ttt, so the whole family qualifies and nothing outside it does.

    What is the largest value of M=3x+5yM = 3x + 5yM=3x+5y on the region cut out by x≥0x \ge 0x≥0, y≥0y \ge 0y≥0, 5x+2y≤405x + 2y \le 405x+2y≤40 and x+2y≤24x + 2y \le 24x+2y≤24?

    Answer choices for question 9

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Checks only the corners that sit on an axis, so (0,12)(0, 12)(0,12) wins and the crossing of the two slanted boundaries is never solved for.

    You chose C: Stops at (8,0)(8, 0)(8,0), where the first limit is spent exactly, on the assumption that using a limit up completely is what optimizes.

    You chose D: Takes (0,20)(0, 20)(0,20), where 5x+2y=405x + 2y = 405x+2y=40 meets the vertical axis, as a corner without testing it against x+2y≤24x + 2y \le 24x+2y≤24, which 404040 breaks.

    The corners are the origin, the two feasible axis points, and the crossing of the slanted boundaries. Subtracting x+2y=24x + 2y = 24x+2y=24 from 5x+2y=405x + 2y = 405x+2y=40 gives 4x=164x = 164x=16, so that crossing is (4,10)(4, 10)(4,10), which satisfies both limits.

    M(0,0)=0,M(8,0)=24,M(0,12)=60,M(4,10)=62M(0,0) = 0, \quad M(8,0) = 24, \quad M(0,12) = 60, \quad M(4,10) = 62M(0,0)=0,M(8,0)=24,M(0,12)=60,M(4,10)=62

    The region is bounded with solid boundaries, so the largest of the corner values is the largest value anywhere.

    Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course.

    A system of three equations in three unknowns has coefficient determinant D=0D = 0D=0. What follows about its solutions?

    Answer choices for question 10

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Reads a vanishing determinant as a verdict of inconsistency, when it only rules a single solution out.

    You chose B: Reads a vanishing determinant as dependence, when a contradiction is equally available to it.

    You chose C: Separates the failure of one method from the system's own behaviour, as though DDD only blocked a route to an answer that is still there.

    The determinant is the quantity every unknown is divided by, so a nonzero value is exactly the condition for one forced answer. A zero value withdraws that condition and nothing more.

    D=0  ⟹  not unique: either none, or infinitely manyD = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{not unique: either none, or infinitely many}D=0⟹not unique: either none, or infinitely many

    Which of the two it is depends on the constants, which DDD never looks at, so the constants have to be compared or the system reduced.

    At which values of kkk does the system 5x+ky=205x + ky = 205x+ky=20 together with kx+5y=15kx + 5y = 15kx+5y=15 have a solution set that is not a single point, and what is that set there?

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Takes one root of 25−k2=025 - k^2 = 025−k2=0 and assumes a vanishing determinant means the two equations describe one line.

    You chose B: Finds both roots but reads a vanishing determinant as dependence, without comparing the constants 202020 and 151515.

    You chose D: Assumes the two roots must behave in opposite ways, one emptying the set and the other collapsing the equations onto each other.

    The coefficient determinant is 25−k225 - k^225−k2, which vanishes at k=5k = 5k=5 and at k=−5k = -5k=−5, so those are the only values where a single point is off the table. Now look at what each one leaves.

    k=5: x+y=4 and x+y=3,k=−5: x−y=4 and x−y=−3k = 5: \ x + y = 4 \ \text{and} \ x + y = 3, \qquad k = -5: \ x - y = 4 \ \text{and} \ x - y = -3k=5: x+y=4 and x+y=3,k=−5: x−y=4 and x−y=−3

    Each value forces one expression to equal two different numbers, so both are inconsistent and neither produces a line.

    On the region cut out by x≥0x \ge 0x≥0, y≥0y \ge 0y≥0, 2x+3y≥242x + 3y \ge 242x+3y≥24 and 4x+y≥184x + y \ge 184x+y≥18, what is true of C=5x+2yC = 5x + 2yC=5x+2y?

    Answer choices for question 14

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reads an unbounded region as removing both extremes, when it removes only the one lying in the direction the region runs.

    You chose C: Takes the largest of the corner values as a largest value, though a corner attains an optimum only once one is known to exist.

    You chose D: Reads x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and y≥0y \ge 0y≥0 as putting the origin in the region, though 2(0)+3(0)≥242(0) + 3(0) \ge 242(0)+3(0)≥24 fails.

    The corners are (0,18)(0, 18)(0,18), the crossing (3,6)(3, 6)(3,6) of the two slanted boundaries, and (12,0)(12, 0)(12,0); each satisfies both requirements.

    C(0,18)=36,C(3,6)=27,C(12,0)=60C(0,18) = 36, \qquad C(3,6) = 27, \qquad C(12,0) = 60C(0,18)=36,C(3,6)=27,C(12,0)=60

    Comparing corner values cannot by itself produce a smallest value on a region that runs on forever, so bound CCC from the two requirements instead. Both weights below are positive, so both inequalities may be used:

    5x+2y=310(2x+3y)+1110(4x+y)≥310(24)+1110(18)=275x + 2y = \tfrac{3}{10}\left(2x + 3y\right) + \tfrac{11}{10}\left(4x + y\right) \ge \tfrac{3}{10}(24) + \tfrac{11}{10}(18) = 275x+2y=103​(2x+3y)+1011​(4x+y)≥103​(24)+1011​(18)=27

    No allowable point brings CCC below 272727, and (3,6)(3, 6)(3,6) reaches it, so 272727 is the smallest value and a corner attains it. Up and to the right the region runs on without limit and CCC grows with it, so there is no largest value.

    A system of four equations in xxx, yyy and zzz reduces to [120501−1100130000]\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right]​1000​2100​0−110​5130​​. What is its solution set?

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads the zero row as freeing a variable, though all three variable columns already carry a pivot of their own.

    You chose B: Reads the zero row as a contradiction, which would need a nonzero constant behind the bar.

    You chose D: Reads each unknown straight off its own row's constant instead of climbing and substituting.

    What does the coefficient determinant of x+2y+4z=3x + 2y + 4z = 3x+2y+4z=3, 2x−y+z=52x - y + z = 52x−y+z=5, 3x+y+5z=83x + y + 5z = 83x+y+5z=8 report?

    Answer choices for question 16

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Adds the three first-row terms rather than alternating their signs, reaching −6+14+20-6 + 14 + 20−6+14+20.

    You chose C: Reads a vanishing determinant as inconsistency, when it only rules a single solution out.

    You chose D: Copies the middle coefficient of the second equation as +1+1+1, losing the minus sign that 2x−y+z=52x - y + z = 52x−y+z=5 carries, and expands the altered grid.

    Expand along the first row, minding the minus on the middle term.

    D=1(−6)−2(7)+4(5)=−6−14+20=0D = 1(-6) - 2(7) + 4(5) = -6 - 14 + 20 = 0D=1(−6)−2(7)+4(5)=−6−14+20=0

    So the answer is not a single triple. Adding the first two equations gives 3x+y+5z=83x + y + 5z = 83x+y+5z=8, which is the third exactly, so the third constrains nothing and two genuine equations remain in three unknowns: infinitely many solutions.

    Which point below is a corner of the region satisfying x≥0x \ge 0x≥0, y≥0y \ge 0y≥0, 2x+5y≤602x + 5y \le 602x+5y≤60 and 4x+5y≤804x + 5y \le 804x+5y≤80?

    Answer choices for question 17

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Reaches x=10x = 10x=10 from the two slanted boundaries but substitutes it back as xxx rather than 4x4x4x, solving 10+5y=8010 + 5y = 8010+5y=80.

    You chose B: Takes the point where 2x+5y=602x + 5y = 602x+5y=60 meets the horizontal axis as a corner, though 4(30)=1204(30) = 1204(30)=120 breaks the other limit.

    You chose C: Reads each limit on its own, so the highest point 4x+5y≤804x + 5y \le 804x+5y≤80 allows on the vertical axis is taken as a corner, though 5(16)=805(16) = 805(16)=80 breaks the other limit.

    A crossing of two boundary lines counts as a corner only when it satisfies every constraint in the system, not merely the two whose lines meet there. Subtracting 2x+5y=602x + 5y = 602x+5y=60 from 4x+5y=804x + 5y = 804x+5y=80 gives 2x=202x = 202x=20, so x=10x = 10x=10, and then 5y=60−205y = 60 - 205y=60−20 gives y=8y = 8y=8.

    2(10)+5(8)=60 ✓,4(10)+5(8)=80 ✓,10≥0, 8≥0 ✓2(10) + 5(8) = 60 \ \checkmark, \qquad 4(10) + 5(8) = 80 \ \checkmark, \qquad 10 \ge 0, \ 8 \ge 0 \ \checkmark2(10)+5(8)=60 ✓,4(10)+5(8)=80 ✓,10≥0, 8≥0 ✓

    Every constraint holds, so (10,8)(10, 8)(10,8) is a corner. The two crossings with the axes fail the constraint they did not come from: (30,0)(30, 0)(30,0) needs 4(30)=1204(30) = 1204(30)=120 to be at most 808080, and (0,16)(0, 16)(0,16) needs 5(16)=805(16) = 805(16)=80 to be at most 606060, so neither is even in the region.

    Now the three ratios can be compared in order. The first two agree, which removes the one-solution case and leaves parallel or coincident; the constant ratio then chooses between them:

    412=−7−21=2163=13.\frac{4}{12} = \frac{-7}{-21} = \frac{21}{63} = \frac{1}{3}.124​=−21−7​=6321​=31​.

    All three agree, so the second equation is the first multiplied through by 333: one line, described twice, and infinitely many solutions.

    Part B

    Both equations reduce to the one line 4x−7y=214x - 7y = 214x−7y=21, so hand a letter to xxx and let yyy follow. Choosing x=7tx = 7tx=7t keeps the division by 777 clean, and 7t7t7t still reaches every real number as ttt does:

    4(7t)−7y=21  ⟹  7y=28t−21  ⟹  y=4t−3.4(7t) - 7y = 21 \;\Longrightarrow\; 7y = 28t - 21 \;\Longrightarrow\; y = 4t - 3.4(7t)−7y=21⟹7y=28t−21⟹y=4t−3.

    Now test the general member in both originals, with the letter still in place:

    Part C

    The size of the numbers. Scaling both sides of an equation by a nonzero constant is one of the moves that never touches a solution set: a pair satisfying 4x−7y=214x - 7y = 214x−7y=21 satisfies 12x−21y=6312x - 21y = 6312x−21y=63, and dividing by 333 walks it back. So the second equation is the first with every number tripled, and the line is the same line.

    3(4x−7y)=3(21)  ⟺  12x−21y=63.3\left(4x - 7y\right) = 3(21) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 12x - 21y = 63.3(4x−7y)=3(21)⟺12x−21y=63.

    Watch out. Producing several shared pairs would settle it, since two distinct shared points force the lines to coincide. One never does.

    The answer

    (0,18)(0, 18)(0,18) breaks the wall limit, since 0+4(18)=720 + 4(18) = 720+4(18)=72 exceeds 323232, and (32,0)(32, 0)(32,0) breaks the budget, since 3(32)=963(32) = 963(32)=96 exceeds 363636.

    The corners are (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0), (12,0)(12, 0)(12,0), (8,6)(8, 6)(8,6) and (0,8)(0, 8)(0,8).     A corner off both axes is where the two slanted boundaries meet, so solve them as equations. Doubling the first and subtracting the second clears yyy:

    2(3x+2y)−(x+4y)=2(36)−32  ⟹  5x=40  ⟹  x=8,2(3x + 2y) - (x + 4y) = 2(36) - 32 \;\Longrightarrow\; 5x = 40 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 8,2(3x+2y)−(x+4y)=2(36)−32⟹5x=40⟹x=8,

    Part B

    Set one variable to zero in each boundary equation, then test the point that comes out against the constraint it did not come from.

    3(0)+2y=36⇒(0,18),x+4(0)=32⇒(32,0).3(0) + 2y = 36 \Rightarrow (0, 18), \qquad x + 4(0) = 32 \Rightarrow (32, 0).3(0)+2y=36⇒(0,18),x+4(0)=32⇒(32,0).

    At (0,18)(0, 18)(0,18) the wall used is 0+4(18)=720 + 4(18) = 720+4(18)=72 metres against a ceiling of 323232. At (32,0)(32, 0)(32,0) the cost is 3(32)=963(32) = 963(32)=96 hundred dollars against a ceiling of 363636. Each point satisfies the one boundary it was built from and fails the other, so neither is an allowable order at all, let alone a corner.

    The test itself. A boundary line records where one constraint is met exactly, so a crossing is guaranteed to satisfy the two constraints that produced it and is guaranteed nothing about the rest. The region is the overlap of all four half-planes, so membership is decided by all four, and a crossing joins the corner list only after every constraint has been checked against it.

    Part A

    x−2y+4z=−8x - 2y + 4z = -8x−2y+4z=−8, then y−z=4y - z = 4y−z=4, then −6z=−6-6z = -6−6z=−6.

    (x,y,z)=(−2,5,1)(x, y, z) = (-2, 5, 1)(x,y,z)=(−2,5,1), and the three original left-hand sides come out as −2-2−2, −8-8−8 and 121212, matching their right-hand sides.

    The first half is right and the second wrong. Any unknown may be cleared first. But each step replaces one equation by itself plus a multiple of another, which neither loses nor invents a solution, so the answer cannot move. The shape turns on how many rows survive as constraints, a property of the equations, not of the route.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Subtract multiples of equation (2)(2)(2) from the other two, so that xxx leaves both at once:

    (1)−3(2): 7y−13z=22,(3)−2(2): 7y−7z=28  ⟹  y−z=4.(1) - 3(2): \ 7y - 13z = 22, \qquad (3) - 2(2): \ 7y - 7z = 28 \;\Longrightarrow\; y - z = 4.(1)−3(2): 7y−13z=22,(3)−2(2): 7y−7z=28⟹y−z=4.

    Now clear yyy from the first of those using the simplified second one:

    (7y−13z)−7(y−z)=22−28  ⟹  −6z=−6.\left(7y - 13z\right) - 7\left(y - z\right) = 22 - 28 \;\Longrightarrow\; -6z = -6.(7y−13z)−7(y−z)=22−28⟹−6z=−6.

    x− 2y+ 4z=−8y− z=4−6z=−6\begin{array}{rrrcr} x & -\, 2y & +\, 4z & = & -8 \\ & y & -\, z & = & 4 \\ & & -6z & = & -6 \end{array}x​−2yy​+4z−z−6z​===​−84−6​

    Part B

    The bottom row gives zzz outright, and each row above brings in exactly one unknown that is not yet known:

    −6z=−6⇒z=1,y−1=4⇒y=5,x−10+4=−8⇒x=−2.-6z = -6 \Rightarrow z = 1, \qquad y - 1 = 4 \Rightarrow y = 5, \qquad x - 10 + 4 = -8 \Rightarrow x = -2.−6z=−6⇒z=1,y−1=4⇒y=5,x−10+4=−8⇒x=−2.

    Now test the triple everywhere, above all in equation (1)(1)(1), which the sweep combined and then set aside:

    3(−2)+5−1=−2 ✓,−2−10+4=−8 ✓,−4+15+1=12 ✓.3(-2) + 5 - 1 = -2 \ \checkmark, \qquad -2 - 10 + 4 = -8 \ \checkmark, \qquad -4 + 15 + 1 = 12 \ \checkmark.3(−2)+5−1=−2 ✓,−2−10+4=−8 ✓,−4+15+1=12 ✓.

    Part C

    The first half. Nothing privileges xxx. Clearing yyy first would use equation (1)(1)(1), whose yyy has coefficient 111, to remove yyy from the other two, and the sweep would run to a staircase in a different order of unknowns. It is a route, not a rule.

    The second half. Each combination replaces one equation by itself plus a multiple of another while leaving the supplier standing, and that step is reversible, so the system after it has exactly the solutions the system before it had:

    Ei→Ei+kEj with Ej kept⟹same solution set.E_i \to E_i + kE_j \ \text{with} \ E_j \ \text{kept} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{same solution set}.Ei​→Ei​+kEj​ with Ej​ kept⟹same solution set.

    A chain of such steps therefore ends on the same set whichever chain it was. Any two honest sweeps of this system land on (−2,5,1)(-2, 5, 1)(−2,5,1).

    What the shape does depend on. Three rows survive here as genuine constraints, so there are three pivots and 3−3=03 - 3 = 03−3=0 free unknowns, which is what makes the answer a single point. A different route would still find three, because whether an equation restates the others is a fact about the equations.

    In one line

The classmate is half right: any unknown may be cleared first, but the answer cannot move, because every step of a sweep replaces one equation by itself plus a multiple of another while keeping the supplier, which neither loses nor invents a solution. What fixes the shape is the number of rows that still constrain, three here, so no unknown is free and the solution set is the single point.

    5. One number computed first, and how much of the answer it is entitled to give . 15 points. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course. Question 5 of 10.

    15 pts Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course.

    Two systems are put side by side. System I is 9x−4y=56,7x+5y=3.9x - 4y = 56, \qquad 7x + 5y = 3.9x−4y=56,7x+5y=3. System II is x+3y−2z=5,2x+6y−4z=9,4x−y+z=3.x + 3y - 2z = 5, \qquad 2x + 6y - 4z = 9, \qquad 4x - y + z = 3.x+3y−2z=5,2x+6y−4z=9,4x−y+z=3. In each case the coefficient determinant is computed before anything else, because it decides how much further there is to go.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Evaluate the coefficient determinant of System I, and then solve the system by forming the two column-swapped determinants and dividing. Check the pair you get in both equations.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Evaluate System II's coefficient determinant by a first-row cofactor expansion, writing out all three minors together with the sign each one carries. Then say what that value settles and what, if anything, it leaves open.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Decide which of the two outcomes System II actually has. Then change exactly one of its constants so that it has the other one instead, and say why no change to any constant could ever give it exactly one solution.

      Carry your own answer forward Continue from whatever value you produced in part B, and say honestly what it does and does not permit. The credit here is for choosing between the two outcomes with the constants, for producing a repair that reaches the other one, and for the argument about what the determinant is built from.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    The answer

    Part A

    The coefficient determinant is 737373, the swapped determinants are 292292292 and −365-365−365, and the solution is (x,y)=(4,−5)(x, y) = (4, -5)(x,y)=(4,−5), which returns 565656 and 333 in the two equations.

    • x=4x = 4x=4 with y=−5y = -5y=−5 is the same pair; (73292, 73−365)\left(\tfrac{73}{292},\ \tfrac{73}{-365}\right)(29273​, −36573​) is not, since it divides the coefficient determinant by the swapped one rather than the other way round

    Part B

    The coefficient determinant is 000. That settles that the solution is not a single triple, and it leaves open which of the other two outcomes holds: no solution, or infinitely many.

    Part C

    System II has no solution: its second equation has twice the first's left side while 999 is not twice 555, so subtracting leaves 0=−10 = -10=−1. Replacing that 999 by 101010 vanishes the row instead, leaving two constraints in three unknowns and a line of solutions. No constant can buy one solution: the determinant reads the coefficients alone.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Take the main diagonal first, then subtract the anti-diagonal, keeping the signs of the entries:

    D=∣9−475∣=45−(−28)=73.D = \begin{vmatrix} 9 & -4 \\ 7 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 45 - (-28) = 73.D=​97​−45​​=45−(−28)=73.

    Since DDD is not zero, one solution exists and the division below is legal. Replace the first column with the constants for the xxx numerator, and the second column for the yyy numerator:

    Dx=∣56−435∣=280+12=292,Dy=∣95673∣=27−392=−365.D_x = \begin{vmatrix} 56 & -4 \\ 3 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 280 + 12 = 292, \qquad D_y = \begin{vmatrix} 9 & 56 \\ 7 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 27 - 392 = -365.Dx​=​563​−45​​=280+12=292,Dy​=​97​563​​=27−392=−365.

    Dividing gives x=29273=4x = \tfrac{292}{73} = 4x=73292​=4 and y=−36573=−5y = \tfrac{-365}{73} = -5y=73−365​=−5. The check holds: 9(4)−4(−5)=569(4) - 4(-5) = 569(4)−4(−5)=56 and 7(4)+5(−5)=37(4) + 5(-5) = 37(4)+5(−5)=3.

    Part B

    Expand along the top row, with the signs running plus, minus, plus, and the middle term genuinely subtracted:

    1∣6−4−11∣−3∣2−441∣+(−2)∣264−1∣=1(2)−3(18)−2(−26)=2−54+52=0.1\begin{vmatrix} 6 & -4 \\ -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} - 3\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + (-2)\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 4 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 1(2) - 3(18) - 2(-26) = 2 - 54 + 52 = 0.1​6−1​−41​​−3​24​−41​​+(−2)​24​6−1​​=1(2)−3(18)−2(−26)=2−54+52=0.

    The determinant is built from the nine coefficients and never looks at the constants, so a value of 000 can only report that the answer is not one triple. Choosing between an empty set and an infinite one needs the constants, which this number has not read.

    Part C

    Which outcome. Compare the first two equations. Their left sides are locked in a ratio, so the constants decide:

    (2)−2(1): 0=9−10=−1.(2) - 2(1): \ 0 = 9 - 10 = -1.(2)−2(1): 0=9−10=−1.

    A false row empties the solution set, whatever the third equation does, so System II has no solution.

    The repair. Replace the 999 by 101010. The same combination then gives 0=00 = 00=0, the second equation is revealed as the first restated, and what survives is x+3y−2z=5x + 3y - 2z = 5x+3y−2z=5 together with 4x−y+z=34x - y + z = 34x−y+z=3: two genuine constraints in three unknowns, so one unknown is free and the solutions form a line.

    Why one solution is out of reach. The coefficient determinant reads the nine coefficients and nothing else. Moving a constant leaves all nine where they are, so DDD stays 000 and the answer stays not-unique. Only a change to a coefficient could restore a single triple.

    In one line

    System I has coefficient determinant 737373, so it has one solution, and the swapped determinants 292292292 and −365-365−365 give (x,y)=(4,−5)(x, y) = (4, -5)(x,y)=(4,−5), which returns 565656 and 333 in the two equations. System II has coefficient determinant 000, which settles only that its answer is not a single triple. The constants decide the rest: the second equation carries twice the first's left side while 999 is not twice 555, so the combination leaves 0=−10 = -10=−1 and there is no solution. Replacing that 999 by 101010 vanishes the row instead and leaves two constraints in three unknowns, a whole line of solutions. No constant at all can restore a single solution, because the determinant reads the nine coefficients and never the constants, so it stays 000 throughout.

    15 pts

    A region of the plane is the quadrilateral with corners (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0), (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0), (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4) and (0,7)(0, 7)(0,7). All four of its sides are solid. Two of them lie along the axes; the other two are the segment from (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0) to (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4) and the segment from (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4) to (0,7)(0, 7)(0,7).     Part A

    Part B

    The corner values are 000, 727272, 727272 and 424242. The largest is 727272, attained at (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0), at (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4), and at every point of the segment joining them.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Each slanted side supplies one boundary equation, found from the two corners it joins. From (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0) to (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4) the slope is −43-\tfrac{4}{3}−34​, and from (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4) to (0,7)(0, 7)(0,7) it is −12-\tfrac{1}{2}−21​:

The axes supply x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and y≥0y \ge 0y≥0, and every boundary is solid, so every symbol allows equality.

    Part B

    Evaluate at the four corners in turn:

    T(0,0)=0,T(9,0)=72,T(6,4)=48+24=72,T(0,7)=42.T(0,0) = 0, \qquad T(9,0) = 72, \qquad T(6,4) = 48 + 24 = 72, \qquad T(0,7) = 42.T(0,0)=0,T(9,0)=72,T(6,4)=48+24=72,T(0,7)=42.

    Two corners tie at 727272. Because the region is convex, the whole segment between them lies inside it, and TTT is 727272 at every point of that segment: a point ttt of the way along is (9−3t, 4t)\left(9 - 3t,\ 4t\right)(9−3t, 4t), and 8(9−3t)+6(4t)=72−24t+24t=728(9 - 3t) + 6(4t) = 72 - 24t + 24t = 728(9−3t)+6(4t)=72−24t+24t=72 for every ttt from 000 to 111.

    Why the tie happens. For each value of ccc, the set where T=cT = cT=c is the line 8x+6y=c8x + 6y = c8x+6y=c, and all such lines share the slope −43-\tfrac{4}{3}−34​. That is exactly the slope of the side joining (9,0)(9, 0)(9,0) to (6,4)(6, 4)(6,4), since the side lies on 4x+3y=364x + 3y = 364x+3y=36 and T=2(4x+3y)T = 2\left(4x + 3y\right)T=2(4x+3y). So the objective's lines and that side are parallel.

    T=8x+6y=2(4x+3y)≤2(36)=72.T = 8x + 6y = 2\left(4x + 3y\right) \le 2(36) = 72.T=8x+6y=2(4x+3y)≤2(36)=72.

    Sliding the line outward, the last one to meet the region is T=72T = 72T=72, and it does not graze a point: it lies along the whole side.

    Whether the principle breaks. It does not. The corner point principle says that wherever an optimum exists and the region has corners, at least one corner attains it. Here two do, which satisfies that statement comfortably. What would contradict the principle is a maximum attained only at an interior point or only in the middle of a side, and the tie here still reaches both ends of the side.

    Watch out. Evaluating at the corners is still the right procedure when an edge ties. What changes is only the report: the answer is the whole edge, and naming one endpoint understates it.

    15 pts

    A water plant doses two additives into each batch.       Part A.

      Evaluate the cost C=4x+5yC = 4x + 5yC=4x+5y at each of the three corners and report the cheapest allowable dose with its litres and its cost. Then show that no allowable dose at all costs less, by combining the two requirements into a lower bound on CCC.

      Part B.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate says the corner point principle cannot be used on this region at all, because the region is unbounded. Say what the principle does and does not require, and say what boundedness would have added here.

      Carry your own answer forward Argue from your own findings in parts A and B, whatever they were. The credit here is for stating what the principle actually requires and for saying what boundedness supplies, not for a particular cheapest dose.

    The answer

    Part A

    The corner costs are 140140140, 747474 and 848484 dollars, and 4x+5y=117(2x+3y)+27(3x+y)≥744x + 5y = \tfrac{11}{7}(2x + 3y) + \tfrac{2}{7}(3x + y) \ge 744x+5y=711​(2x+3y)+72​(3x+y)≥74, so the cheapest dose is 666 litres of X with 101010 of Y, at 747474 dollars.

    • 747474 dollars at (6,10)(6, 10)(6,10) is the same answer, and any positive weights on the two requirements that combine to 4x+5y4x + 5y4x+5y give the same bound; 747474 on its own is not, because a cost with no dose attached does not tell the plant what to pour

    Part B

    There is none. Take any allowable dose and add a litre of X: both requirements still hold, since more of each impurity is removed, and the cost rises by 444 dollars. So no dose can carry the largest cost. The argument turns on the region running on without limit in that direction.

    Part C

    The principle requires an optimum to exist and the region to have corners; it does not require boundedness. The cheapest dose does exist, and a corner attains it. Boundedness with solid boundaries, on a region that is not empty, would have guaranteed a dearest dose too, and that guarantee is what this region withholds.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Evaluate the cost at each corner in turn, keeping the litres attached to the number:

    C(0,28)=140,C(6,10)=24+50=74,C(21,0)=84.C(0, 28) = 140, \qquad C(6, 10) = 24 + 50 = 74, \qquad C(21, 0) = 84.C(0,28)=140,C(6,10)=24+50=74,C(21,0)=84.

    The smallest of the three is 747474 dollars, at 666 litres of X and 101010 litres of Y, and that dose meets both requirements exactly: 2(6)+3(10)=422(6) + 3(10) = 422(6)+3(10)=42 units of iron and 3(6)+10=283(6) + 10 = 283(6)+10=28 units of manganese.

    Comparing three corner values does not by itself produce a cheapest dose, because the corner principle assumes an optimum exists and this region runs on without limit. So bound the cost from the requirements themselves, using weights that are positive so that both inequalities may be applied:

    4x+5y=117(2x+3y)+27(3x+y)≥117(42)+27(28)=74.4x + 5y = \tfrac{11}{7}\left(2x + 3y\right) + \tfrac{2}{7}\left(3x + y\right) \ge \tfrac{11}{7}(42) + \tfrac{2}{7}(28) = 74.4x+5y=711​(2x+3y)+72​(3x+y)≥711​(42)+72​(28)=74.

    No allowable dose costs less than 747474 dollars, and (6,10)(6, 10)(6,10) costs exactly that, so a cheapest dose does exist and it is the one found.

    Part B

    Suppose some allowable dose (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) carried the largest cost. Move one litre to the right, to (x+1, y)(x + 1,\ y)(x+1, y), and check the requirements:

    2(x+1)+3y=(2x+3y)+2≥42,3(x+1)+y=(3x+y)+3≥28,2(x + 1) + 3y = \left(2x + 3y\right) + 2 \ge 42, \qquad 3(x + 1) + y = \left(3x + y\right) + 3 \ge 28,2(x+1)+3y=(2x+3y)+2≥42,3(x+1)+y=(3x+y)+3≥28,

    and x+1≥0x + 1 \ge 0x+1≥0, y≥0y \ge 0y≥0 still hold. So the new dose is allowable too, and its cost is

    C(x+1, y)=C(x,y)+4>C(x,y).C(x + 1,\ y) = C(x, y) + 4 > C(x, y).C(x+1, y)=C(x,y)+4>C(x,y).

    That contradicts the supposed largest cost, so no dose holds one. What made the step always available is that the requirements are all lower bounds, so nothing caps xxx from above: the region runs on forever to the right, and the cost climbs as it goes.

    Part C

    What the principle asks for. It says that wherever an optimum of a linear objective exists on a region with corners, at least one corner attains it. Existence is a hypothesis, not a conclusion, and boundedness appears nowhere in the statement.

    What boundedness is for. Boundedness together with solid boundaries is what supplies the existence hypothesis, in both directions at once, so long as the region has a point in it to begin with: a nonempty closed bounded region has a largest and a smallest value for any linear objective. Losing boundedness loses that guarantee and nothing else.

    nonempty, bounded and closed  ⟹  both extremes exist  ⟹  a corner attains each\text{nonempty, bounded and closed} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{both extremes exist} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{a corner attains each}nonempty, bounded and closed⟹both extremes exist⟹a corner attains each

    This region. Part B showed the cost is unbounded above, so no dearest dose exists and there is nothing for a corner to attain in that direction. The cheapest dose does exist, since part A bounded the cost below by 747474 dollars and a corner reached that bound, so the principle did its work on the half of the question that had an answer.

    Watch out. The classmate's rule and its opposite are both wrong. Unboundedness never guarantees that an optimum is missing, and it never guarantees that one is present; it only withdraws the guarantee.

    In one line

    The cost C=4x+5yC = 4x + 5yC=4x+5y is 140140140, 747474 and 848484 dollars at (0,28)(0, 28)(0,28), (6,10)(6, 10)(6,10) and (21,0)(21, 0)(21,0), and combining the two requirements as 4x+5y=117(2x+3y)+27(3x+y)≥744x + 5y = \tfrac{11}{7}\left(2x + 3y\right) + \tfrac{2}{7}\left(3x + y\right) \ge 744x+5y=711​(2x+3y)+72​(3x+y)≥74 shows that no allowable dose costs less, so the cheapest dose is 666 litres of X with 101010 litres of Y at 747474 dollars a batch. There is no dearest dose: from any allowable dose, one more litre of X keeps both requirements met and adds 444 dollars, so no dose can hold the largest cost, and what makes that step always available is the region running on without limit to the right. The classmate is wrong about the principle. It requires an optimum to exist and the region to have corners, never boundedness; boundedness with solid boundaries, on a region that is not empty, is merely what would have guaranteed existence in both directions. Here existence holds for the minimum, which the bound above establishes, and fails for the maximum, and the corner that attains the minimum is exactly where the principle says it will be.

  10. 10

    10. One coefficient still to be chosen, and what the determinant makes of it . 16 points. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course. Question 10 of 10.

    16 pts Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course.

    The system 4x−3y=7,kx+6y=24x - 3y = 7, \qquad kx + 6y = 24x−3y=7,kx+6y=2 carries an unspecified number kkk in front of xxx in its second equation, and nowhere else. Every other number in it is fixed.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Express the coefficient determinant in terms of kkk. Say for which kkk a single solution is unavailable, and decide, at any such kkk, which of the two remaining outcomes actually occurs.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      For the values of kkk at which the division is legal, write xxx as a single expression in kkk, simplified as far as it goes, and say what licenses the simplification.

      Carry your own answer forward Divide by whichever coefficient determinant you produced in part A, and exclude whichever value made it vanish. The credit here is for putting the column-swapped determinant on top, for simplifying only where a factor is genuinely nonzero, and for saying which condition licenses that.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 5 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Find the value of kkk for which the solution has x=2x = 2x=2. Then decide whether any value of kkk at all gives this system infinitely many solutions, and argue that decision rather than testing values.

      Carry your own answer forward Solve for kkk using whichever expression for xxx you produced in part B, and argue the second question from the ratios of the system as it is stated. The credit here is for reaching a value of kkk honestly from your own expression, and for an argument that covers every kkk at once rather than a sample of them.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    The answer

    Part A

    The coefficient determinant is 3k+243k + 243k+24, which is zero only at k=−8k = -8k=−8. There the two equations demand 4x−3y=74x - 3y = 74x−3y=7 and 4x−3y=−14x - 3y = -14x−3y=−1 at once, so the system has no solution.

    • 24+3k24 + 3k24+3k or 3(k+8)3(k + 8)3(k+8) is the same expression; a determinant of 24−3k24 - 3k24−3k has taken the anti-diagonal product as +3k+3k+3k rather than −3k-3k−3k, and it puts the failure at the wrong value of kkk

    Part B

    x=483k+24=16k+8x = \dfrac{48}{3k + 24} = \dfrac{16}{k + 8}x=3k+2448​=k+816​, for every kkk other than −8-8−8. Cancelling the 333 is licensed because 333 is nonzero, and the expression exists at all only because k+8k + 8k+8 is.

    • 483(k+8)\frac{48}{3(k + 8)}3(k+8)48​ unsimplified is the same function of kkk; what is not the same is 16k+168\frac{16}{k} + \frac{16}{8}k16​+816​, which splits a single denominator into two

    Part C

    Setting the part B expression equal to 222 gives k+8=8k + 8 = 8k+8=8, so k=0k = 0k=0. No value of kkk gives infinitely many: that needs 4k=−36=72\tfrac{4}{k} = \tfrac{-3}{6} = \tfrac{7}{2}k4​=6−3​=27​, and the last two ratios carry no kkk and are already unequal.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Main diagonal minus anti-diagonal, with the sign of the −3-3−3 carried into the second product:

    D=∣4−3k6∣=24−(−3)k=3k+24.D = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ k & 6 \end{vmatrix} = 24 - (-3)k = 3k + 24.D=​4k​−36​​=24−(−3)k=3k+24.

    This vanishes exactly when k=−8k = -8k=−8, so for every other kkk the system has exactly one solution. At k=−8k = -8k=−8 the second equation reads −8x+6y=2-8x + 6y = 2−8x+6y=2; dividing by −2-2−2 gives

    4x−3y=−1,4x - 3y = -1,4x−3y=−1,

    while the first equation insists the same expression equals 777. Nothing can do both, so the outcome there is no solution.

    Part B

    Replace the first column of the coefficient determinant with the constant column, then divide by the coefficient determinant:

    Dx=∣7−326∣=42+6=48,x=483k+24=483(k+8)=16k+8.D_x = \begin{vmatrix} 7 & -3 \\ 2 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = 42 + 6 = 48, \qquad x = \frac{48}{3k + 24} = \frac{48}{3\left(k + 8\right)} = \frac{16}{k + 8}.Dx​=​72​−36​​=42+6=48,x=3k+2448​=3(k+8)48​=k+816​.

    Factoring 333 out of the denominator is always legal, and cancelling it against the numerator is legal because 333 is not zero. The expression as a whole is defined only where k+8≠0k + 8 \ne 0k+8=0, and that is not an extra assumption: it is the condition part A already imposed before any division was allowed.

    Watch out. The swapped determinant goes on top. Writing DDx\frac{D}{D_x}Dx​D​ instead returns the reciprocal, and here it would report x=k+816x = \frac{k + 8}{16}x=16k+8​, which fails the equations.

    Part C

    The value of kkk. Set the expression from part B equal to 222:

    16k+8=2  ⟹  k+8=8  ⟹  k=0.\frac{16}{k + 8} = 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; k + 8 = 8 \;\Longrightarrow\; k = 0.k+816​=2⟹k+8=8⟹k=0.

    Check it directly. With k=0k = 0k=0 the second equation is 6y=26y = 26y=2, so y=13y = \tfrac{1}{3}y=31​, and the first gives 4x=7+1=84x = 7 + 1 = 84x=7+1=8, that is x=2x = 2x=2.

    Why infinitely many is unreachable. Two equations in two unknowns have infinitely many solutions exactly when one is a rescaling of the other, coefficients and constant alike. Written as ratios, that demands

    4k=−36=72.\frac{4}{k} = \frac{-3}{6} = \frac{7}{2}.k4​=6−3​=27​.

    The last two of those carry no kkk: they are −12-\tfrac{1}{2}−21​ and 72\tfrac{7}{2}27​, fixed numbers that are not equal. So the chain breaks at a link kkk cannot reach, whatever value it is given. The only degenerate case available is therefore the one part A found, where the coefficient ratios line up at k=−8k = -8k=−8 and the constants refuse to follow.

    Reading it back through the determinant. The determinant vanishes only at k=−8k = -8k=−8, so that is the only candidate for a non-unique answer at all, and there the system is inconsistent. That is the determinant test working exactly as advertised: it identifies where uniqueness fails and declines to say which failure it is, and the constants supply the rest.

    In one line

    The coefficient determinant is 3k+243k + 243k+24, which vanishes only at k=−8k = -8k=−8; there the second equation reduces to 4x−3y=−14x - 3y = -14x−3y=−1 against the first equation's 4x−3y=74x - 3y = 74x−3y=7, so the system has no solution. For every other kkk there is exactly one solution, with x=483k+24=483(k+8)=16k+8x = \frac{48}{3k + 24} = \frac{48}{3\left(k + 8\right)} = \frac{16}{k + 8}x=3k+2448​=3(k+8)48​=k+816​: cancelling the factor 333 is licensed by 333 being nonzero, while k+8≠0k + 8 \ne 0k+8=0 is separately what permitted the division in the first place and is where the expression is defined. Setting that equal to 222 gives k=0k = 0k=0, and the system 4x−3y=74x - 3y = 74x−3y=7 with 6y=26y = 26y=2 does return x=2x = 2x=2. No value of kkk produces infinitely many solutions: that would need 4k=−36=72\tfrac{4}{k} = \tfrac{-3}{6} = \tfrac{7}{2}k4​=6−3​=27​, and the last two ratios carry no kkk and are already unequal, so the only degenerate case this system has is the inconsistent one.
